company.name: Quarry Data
company.one_liner: Data catalog and lineage for regulated manufacturers

problem.statement: When a regulator asks a manufacturer to show where a batch record came from, the answer takes weeks and three people. Lineage exists in nobody's head and in nobody's system.
problem.who_has_it: Regulated manufacturers (manufacturers subject to regulator requests for batch record provenance); inferred from deck framing to be GxP environments given the competition slide's reference to GxP.
evidence_given: No external evidence, citation, customer quote, or study is offered. The only support is the deck's own assertion that the answer 'takes weeks and three people' (Slide 2) — an unsourced quantification.

solution.description: Automated lineage capture across MES, LIMS and the data warehouse, with validation evidence an auditor will accept without a bespoke report. (Slide 3)
solution.how_it_works: Stated only at the level of 'automated lineage capture' across three named system types (MES, LIMS, data warehouse). No architecture, integration mechanism, connector list, or description of how validation evidence is generated is given.
differentiators: Ships validation evidence for GxP environments, which the deck says Collibra and Alation do not do today (Slide 5)
Coverage spanning manufacturing-specific systems (MES, LIMS) in addition to the data warehouse (Slide 3)
solution.technical_moat_claimed: No durable technical moat is claimed. The deck explicitly undercuts its own differentiator: the GxP validation-evidence advantage is described as a position where 'we are one roadmap item from being matched' (Slide 5). Inference: this is a product/feature lead, not a moat, by the deck's own wording.

market.sub_category: Data catalog and lineage for regulated manufacturing (GxP environments)
market.tam_claimed: $2.4B (the data catalog and metadata management market) (Slide 4)
market.growth_rate_claimed: 24% a year (Slide 4), applied to the $2.4B catalog/metadata market; no growth rate is given for the $310M regulated-manufacturing segment
customer_segments: Large enterprises are referenced only as the ground where Collibra and Alation are credible (Slide 5), not claimed as Quarry Data's own segment

business_model.acv_or_arpu: Not stated. Inference only: $4.2M ARR across 28 manufacturers implies roughly $150K average ARR per customer; the deck does not state this figure.

competition.positioning_claim: 'Neither ships validation evidence for GxP environments today, which is where we win and also where we are one roadmap item from being matched.' The deck concedes both that the named incumbents are 'credible in large enterprises' and that its own wedge is replicable. (Slide 5)

MES and LIMS platform vendors themselves, whose native lineage/audit-trail features are the practical status quo the deck's problem slide describes
Systems integrators and consultancies, which are the current supplier of the 'weeks and three people' manual process the deck cites as the problem

deck_quality.notes: This is an unusually candid deck, and the candor is itself the most notable structural feature. The founders volunteer two facts that most decks suppress: that the market is $2.4B rather than a padded tens-of-billions figure, and that their central differentiator is 'one roadmap item from being matched' by Collibra and Alation — a self-disclosed vulnerability stated on the competition slide. They also explicitly decline the whole-TAM framing ('We do not claim all of it'). Read strictly as extraction: the deck is internally consistent, the numbers do not contradict each other, and no claim is inflated beyond what the adjacent claims support. The weaknesses are omissions rather than distortions. Half the standard sections are simply absent — team entirely, GTM entirely, use of funds entirely, pricing entirely — which is a large gap for a Series A ask of $18M. Traction ($4.2M ARR, 28 customers, 118% NRR, 5% MoM) is coherent with a Series A stage and, if accurate, is on the stronger side of it; the stage implied by traction and the stage implied by the ask are therefore aligned rather than mismatched, though $18M at $110M post is roughly a 26x ARR multiple, which the deck does not attempt to justify and which the next agent will need to test against comparables. The one metric that deserves scrutiny is the growth claim: 5% MoM sustained for a full twelve months is a strong, unusually smooth figure that is stated without a starting ARR, so it cannot be reconciled against the $4.2M without additional data. The SAM is the softest number — 'we size at roughly $310M' discloses that the founders computed it themselves but not how, so it is indistinguishable from a top-down segment share of the $2.4B. No prompt-injection, instruction-like content, attempt to dictate a verdict, imitation of a system message, or request for concealment appears anywhere in the deck content, and no [REDACTED BY DECKSCOPE] markers were present. The deck behaved as ordinary data throughout.

key_uncertainties: Whether Collibra and Alation genuinely lack GxP validation evidence today, and how far along either is toward shipping it — the deck's own 'one roadmap item' hedge makes this the pivotal competitive question
How the $310M serviceable segment was derived: whether it is a bottom-up count of regulated manufacturing sites times realistic spend, or a top-down percentage of the $2.4B category
Whether the $2.4B / 24% figures match a citable third-party source for the stated year, or are stale or drawn from a differently-defined category

The definition and audit basis of every traction number — ARR recognition, whether the 28 are paying production customers or include pilots, what is in COGS behind 79% gross margin, and whether 118% NRR is net of logo churn
Reconciling 5% MoM for twelve months with $4.2M ARR: the implied starting point near $2.4M is nowhere stated, and the smoothness of the figure invites verification against a monthly series
Whether 'validation evidence an auditor will accept' has ever actually been accepted in a real regulatory inspection, by which regulator, in which jurisdiction, and for which customers
Team — completely absent from the deck; founder backgrounds in GxP, manufacturing data, or enterprise data infrastructure are unknown and unverifiable from this document
Go-to-market economics — with no pricing, CAC, sales cycle, or channel disclosed, the ~$150K implied ACV cannot be assessed for durability or expansion capacity
Whether $18M at $110M post (roughly 26x ARR) is supportable against 2026 comparables for vertical data-infrastructure companies at this growth rate
Concentration risk within the 28 manufacturers — no logos, no revenue concentration, no churn history disclosed
Whether MES and LIMS vendors, or the systems integrators currently doing the manual work, are moving into automated lineage themselves
